title: The Culiacán Clinic That Opened in 2003 With Three Services
dek: A Sinaloa businessman who had nearly lost a son put cheap diagnostic tests in one place and built the clinic to pay its own way.

story.event: Opening the first low-cost, non-profit diagnostic clinic in Culiacán
story.summary: In October 2003 Jesús Vizcarra Calderón, a Sinaloa businessman whose family owns the meat company SuKarne and who had just been elected to Mexico's Congress, opened the first Salud Digna clinic in central Culiacán, a non-profit offering cheap diagnostic tests. He paid for the start himself but designed it to live on its fees; it covered its costs from about 2007, opened its next clinics five years after the first, and by 2024 had more than 200 clinics in Mexico.
paragraphs: In October 2003 a small clinic opened in the centre of Culiacán, capital of the Mexican state of Sinaloa, offering medical tests priced for people who could not afford private laboratories. Behind it was Jesús Vizcarra Calderón, chairman of the family group that owns the meat company SuKarne, newly elected to Mexico's Congress. His wife, Alma Avendaño de Vizcarra, was the organisation's first president. Vizcarra has said it started with only three services.

The idea had a long fuse. Years earlier his youngest son had fallen gravely ill as a small child. Vizcarra told the columnist Barbara Anderson it was a brain tumour found when the boy was four; in a later interview he called it a stroke. The family flew the boy to Tucson, in the United States, and he recovered. Afterwards, Anderson reports, Vizcarra asked himself what would have happened had they depended on a local clinic. He set up two foundations which, by his own account, went badly, then became president of the board of Culiacán's Civil Hospital, known, he said, as the hospital of death. There, he said, he learned how much rests on early diagnosis.

The clinic grew out of his political office, whose staff had been arranging medical help for poor districts of the city. By the organisation's account, demand outgrew what they could offer and people could not wait. The answer was to put diagnostic services in one fixed place and charge for them, cheaply. Vizcarra paid for the start with his own money, but Salud Digna was set up as a non-profit association meant to cover its costs from its fees and reinvest any surplus. His motto, which opens a Harvard Business School case on the organisation, was "Don't tell me why not; tell me how to."

Growth was slow at first: five years passed before the next clinics opened, in Los Mochis and Guasave. A 2011 summary of the Harvard case said the organisation had been financially independent since 2007 while charging about a third of private clinics' rates, and had 14 clinics. By 2024 it had more than 200 clinics across Mexico and reported more than 18 million patients a year. The family has since placed it in a trust so that, Vizcarra says, it can never be sold.

quote.text: he will have an easily opened pocket, but not one with a hole in it, so that much may be taken out of it, yet nothing may fall out of it.
quote.work: Of a Happy Life (De Vita Beata), in the Minor Dialogues
quote.source_title: Minor Dialogues, Together With the Dialogue on Clemency, tr. Aubrey Stewart, Project Gutenberg eBook #64576
quote.connection: Vizcarra's first two foundations went badly; the clinic he opened in 2003 asked each patient for a little and was built to pay its own way. Seneca's picture of the wise giver is a pocket that opens easily but has no hole in it: generosity that lasts because it is looked after.

reflection: There is a kind of generosity that empties itself quickly: the free favour that becomes expected, the unpaid evening, the help that leaves nothing for tomorrow. We do not know why Vizcarra's first two foundations failed. We do know that what he built next asked something small of everyone it served and used it to keep the doors open.

You give a great deal, at work and at home. Seneca does not tell you to give less. He tells you to look for the hole in the pocket, the place where what you give drains away without reaching anyone. Finding it is not meanness. It is how giving lasts.
invitation: Think of one thing you give often, perhaps an hour of help or a regular favour, and ask where part of it leaks away without reaching anyone. Mend only that part this week.

sources.title: Salud Digna: historia de la red de laboratorios
sources.supports: Salud Digna is a non-profit civil association born in 2003; the first clinic opened in Culiacán in October 2003 under Jesús Vizcarra Calderón, chairman of Grupo VIZ; five years later it extended to Los Mochis and Guasave; nearly 200 clinics after twenty years; the Vizcarra family owns SuKarne; Vizcarra was a federal deputy (2003–2004).

sources.title: El CEO de Salud Digna explica por qué sus precios son tan bajos sin perder calidad y cómo seguirán creciendo
sources.supports: Founded in 2003 after Vizcarra's four-year-old son was diagnosed with a tumour; at its creation financed with Vizcarra's personal funds and designed from the start to become self-sufficient, reinvesting everything it earns; about 240 clinics and 14,000 staff in 2025; the board declined an Inter-American Development Bank loan.

sources.title: La nueva era de Salud Digna (Anderson Report)
sources.supports: Vizcarra's account that 25 years earlier his four-year-old son Raúl was found to have a brain tumour; the family flew him to Tucson and his life was saved; Vizcarra asked himself what would have happened at a local clinic; invited to the Civil Hospital of Culiacán, known as 'the hospital of death', he became president of its board; his view that early diagnosis is everything, the focus of his work since 2003; 235 clinics and more than 18 million patients a year in 2024.

sources.title: El derrame cerebral de su hijo lo cambió todo… hoy su proyecto atiende a millones en México
sources.publisher: Tus Buenas Noticias (7 April 2026), reporting Vizcarra's interview with Sabina Berman
sources.supports: Vizcarra's account that his son suffered a stroke more than thirty years earlier; he created two foundations that went badly before being invited to the Civil Hospital of Culiacán, where he learned the importance of early diagnosis; after his election as a deputy in 2003 he started his first clinic, with only three services; it became self-sufficient within its first five years; the family trust designed so it is never sold; more than 240 clinics in 2026.

sources.title: Este trágico suceso impulsó a Jesús Vizcarra a fundar Salud Digna
sources.supports: Vizcarra's own words in the Sabina Berman interview that his youngest son had a stroke 'about 36 years ago' and recovered, and that it changed his life; Salud Digna founded in 2003 as a non-profit civil association focused on prevention and early diagnosis.

sources.title: Salud Digna, Harvard University Case Study
sources.publisher: Salud Digna press release via PR Newswire (Culiacán, 28 January 2011)
sources.supports: Founded in 2003 as a non-profit; Harvard Business School case study opening with Vizcarra's motto 'Don't tell me why not; tell me how to'; 14 clinics in 2011; financially independent since 2007 with rates a third of private clinics'; began as the management office of then federal representative Vizcarra providing medical support for poor neighbourhoods, and when demand grew and people could not wait, diagnostic services were placed in one fixed location in 2003; Alma Avendaño de Vizcarra the first president.

sources.title: Salud Digna: Historia de éxito sinaloense, ¿cómo nació y por qué es tan importante?
sources.supports: Salud Digna began in 2003 as Vizcarra's initiative after health days in Culiacán neighbourhoods offering spectacles and clinical analysis; first branch opened in October 2003 in the state capital; five years later Los Mochis, then Guasave; Baja California in 2009 and Mexico City in 2013.

sources.title: Salud Digna: quién es el dueño de estos laboratorios
sources.supports: Founder and owner Jesús Vizcarra Calderón, also owner of SuKarne; in October 2003, with his family, he opened the first Salud Digna clinical laboratory in Culiacán; second and third branches in Los Mochis and Guasave five years later.

sources.title: Salud Digna, ¿cómo hace para dar precios bajos y qué estrategia tiene a futuro?
sources.supports: First clinic in central Culiacán; the founder's son fell gravely ill 25 years earlier (per the chief executive); between 218 and 222 clinics in Mexico in 2024, after reaching 100 only in 2019; more than 18 million people served; equipment supplied by partner companies in exchange for reagent purchases.

sources.title: Una inusual alianza para llevar salud visual a todo el país
sources.supports: Salud Digna para Todos offers low-cost tests to the base of the pyramid; created by Jesús Vizcarra; 31 clinics and one in Los Angeles in March 2015; its statement that Salud Digna was created at the end of 2014 is an error; a case study at Harvard Business School and IPADE.

cross_checks.claim: Jesús Vizcarra Calderón founded Salud Digna, whose first clinic opened in Culiacán in October 2003.
The clinic grew out of medical outreach to poor neighbourhoods organised from Vizcarra's office.
Started with Vizcarra's own money as a non-profit designed to sustain itself, it became financially independent within about five years.
A grave brain illness of Vizcarra's young son preceded the founding (described as a tumour in some accounts and a stroke in others).
At Culiacán's Civil Hospital Vizcarra came to see the importance of early diagnosis.
The next clinics opened five years later, in Los Mochis and Guasave.
By 2024 Salud Digna had more than 200 clinics and more than 18 million patients a year.
Salud Digna was the subject of a Harvard Business School case study.

research_notes: Founder: every source names Jesús Vizcarra Calderón as founder; the 2011 release names his wife, Alma Avendaño de Vizcarra, as first president and their daughter Lucero Vizcarra Avendaño as president from 2007, and Telediario says he opened the first clinic 'with his family'. The story names Vizcarra as founder and his wife as first president. The son's illness: Vizcarra told El Financiero (2024) it was a brain tumour found in his son Raúl at four, 25 years earlier (about 1999); Expansión (2025, quoting the chief executive) also says tumour; in the 2026 Sabina Berman interview, as reported by Tus Buenas Noticias and quoted by Luz Noticias, he said his youngest son had a stroke about 36 years earlier (about 1990). The story gives both descriptions, attributed, and does not date the illness. Luz Noticias's first article (7 April 2026) implies the illness was the immediate trigger in 2003; Vizcarra's own account puts two failed foundations and the Civil Hospital in between, which the story follows. Founding date: Expansión, Telediario and Tus Buenas Noticias say October 2003; an SDP Noticias opinion column says October 2002; Forbes México (March 2015) says 'finales de 2014', an evident error since the same article already reports 31 clinics; the story uses October 2003. Self-sufficiency: the 2011 release summarising the Harvard case says financially independent since 2007; Vizcarra says within the first five years; consistent. Outcome numbers vary with date and source: 14 clinics (2011 release), 31 (Forbes México, March 2015), 100 in 2019 and 218–222 in mid-2024 (Publimetro), 235 in the same week (El Financiero), about 240 (Expansión 2025, Tus Buenas Noticias 2026); patients 'more than 18 million' a year in 2024 (El Financiero and Publimetro agree), 23 million in 2026 (Tus Buenas Noticias), 'almost 3 million a month' (Expansión 2025). The story uses 'more than 200 clinics' and 'more than 18 million patients a year' for 2024, the figures on which two sources agree. Daily patient figures (90,000 to 100,000) are not used. Inter-American Development Bank: Forbes México says Salud Digna received IDB loans; Expansión (2025) quotes the chief executive saying the board declined an IDB loan offer; not used. Spanish-language quotations from Vizcarra are paraphrased, not translated inside quotation marks; the only direct quotation is the English motto in the 2011 release. Editor's note: an SDP Noticias opinion column repeats rumours that Vizcarra is a compadre of the cartel figure Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada and voices rival laboratories' complaints that Salud Digna's non-profit status is an unfair advantage; the column itself presents them as hearsay, and nothing in the other cited reporting substantiates them. They are not part of this episode and are not mentioned, but the editor may wish to weigh them. Mexico News Daily's profile was blocked (403) and is not cited. The two Expansión URLs from 2023 and 2024 serve the same article; only one is cited. The Seneca passage describes how the wise man should handle wealth and giving; it is applied to an organisation by analogy.
